paper.title: Language to Rewards for Robotic Skill Synthesis
paper.source_version: CoRL 2023 final, PMLR 229:374-404; PDF SHA-256 5088126171bc422d33b6cccd0169e371db11ecce79ff6355b22d81a9b095dbae; arXiv:2306.08647v2

decision_relevance.why_admitted: The paper gives a source-located language-to-executable-reward interface, a two-stage structured compiler, repeated candidate evaluation, and multi-turn language correction while treating the downstream robot optimizer as fixed within each embodiment. These mechanisms directly inform Sam's task-reward and steering contracts.
not_evidence_for: Reference-dataset composition, oracle synthesis, mode transitions, or OGMP behavior
Improved learned-policy training under PPO, SONIC, VIBE, or any other fixed RL trainer
Free-form reward-program synthesis beyond a predefined residual/API vocabulary
A reward-only causal effect across embodiments with identical scene, observations, actions, dynamics, and controller
Quantified real-world reliability, safety, calibration, or hardware success rate
A complete public reproduction of the manipulator, real-robot, or moonwalk results

mechanisms.name: Language-to-reward interface
mechanisms.description: Human instructions and corrections are translated into reward parameters and weights rather than directly into low-level actions or a sequence of fixed skills.

mechanisms.name: Structured Motion Descriptor
mechanisms.description: A first GPT-4 call expands a potentially vague instruction into a morphology-specific natural-language template with typed choices, numeric slots, and optional fields.

mechanisms.name: Constrained Reward Coder
mechanisms.description: A second GPT-4 call maps the structured motion description to Python calls from a predefined reward API; the prompt supplies API documentation, one response-format example, and rules.

mechanisms.name: Parameterized residual reward
mechanisms.description: The controller objective is a negative weighted sum of normalized residuals. The residual library and norms are predefined; the LLM composes terms and changes parameters and weights, including zeroing a term.

mechanisms.name: Fixed MJPC motion controller
mechanisms.description: At each control step, MuJoCo MPC optimizes an action sequence for the current generated reward, executes the current action, observes the next state, and replans; iLQG is used for locomotion and Predictive Sampling for manipulation.

mechanisms.name: Interactive language revision
mechanisms.description: Users observe synthesized motion and issue natural-language corrections or follow-on commands; the upstream translator revises the reward specification while the low-level optimizer remains the execution backend.

mechanisms.name: Repeated candidate evaluation
mechanisms.description: For every task and method, ten generated responses are each evaluated in MJPC fifty times; success and best-of-N pass-rate curves separate code-generation variability from controller variability.

mechanisms.name: Hardware-specific steady-motion regularizer
mechanisms.description: The real-manipulator version adds a hand-designed residual that penalizes high end-effector and joint speed, fast object motion, gripper/object speed mismatch, and inappropriate gripper state because unconstrained simulated MPC found motions beyond the hardware.

mechanisms.name: Pinned Barkour-only public release
mechanisms.description: At commit 4a3a20f, package version 0.0.1 exposes one Barkour task configuration, two-stage/direct/low-level prompt variants, and an MJPC parameter bridge; it is not a release of every embodiment reported in the paper.

mechanisms.name: Confirmed local execution of generated code
mechanisms.description: The public macOS fallback warns that code is untrusted, asks the user to confirm, compiles it, and runs it with the local interpreter; output parameters are subsequently key-filtered and float-cast, but confirmation does not sandbox the code itself.

failure_modes.name: Manual morphology templates
failure_modes.description: Each robot morphology requires a manually designed structured description template, limiting plug-and-play transfer.

failure_modes.name: Language-only expressivity limit
failure_modes.description: Tasks with hard-to-verbalize style targets such as walking gracefully are difficult to specify through the paper's interaction channel.

failure_modes.name: Bounded reward vocabulary
failure_modes.description: Predefined residuals improve translation stability but sacrifice flexibility; the reported system cannot express time-varying rewards without redesigning its prompt and API.

failure_modes.name: Controller variance despite a correct reward
failure_modes.description: Dynamic or precise tasks, including biped standing and upright banana, show higher MJPC outcome variance even when the generated reward is judged correct.

failure_modes.name: Manipulator reward-table ambiguity
failure_modes.description: The final paper's manipulator table appears to pair the target-XY label with a z residual and the target-height label with an xy residual, and it omits the orientation term's default weight.

failure_modes.name: Published/released robot-model mismatch
failure_modes.description: The paper's moonwalk used an older MuJoCo model with unrealistically strong actuators; the official README says moonwalking is impossible in the released model.

failure_modes.name: Partial and mutable release
failure_modes.description: The pinned code exposes only Barkour; the `gpt-4` service alias and `openai` Python dependency are not content-addressed, so the release does not pin the exact language-model behavior or reproduce the full paper suite.

failure_modes.name: Untrusted local code execution
failure_modes.description: The macOS fallback obtains confirmation and then runs model-generated Python with the local interpreter. Later JSON key filtering protects MJPC parameter installation but does not prevent arbitrary actions during code execution.

failure_modes.name: Evaluation uncertainty gap
failure_modes.description: The paper reports repeated rollouts and pass-rate curves but not confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, an immutable evaluator artifact, or a quantified multi-task hardware reliability study.

evaluation.name: Seventeen-category simulated suite
evaluation.description: Nine quadruped categories and eight dexterous-manipulator categories cover semantic heading, poses, limbs, locomotion styles, object interaction, reorientation, and articulated objects, with expected behavior listed separately.

evaluation.name: Ten-by-fifty end-to-end repetition
evaluation.description: Each task-method pair receives ten LLM outputs; every output is evaluated in MJPC fifty times, exposing both reward-generation and controller variability.

evaluation.name: Structured translator ablation and primitive-policy baseline
evaluation.description: The full two-stage system is compared with direct Reward Coder output and Code-as-Policies using three hand-designed primitive skills per embodiment.

evaluation.name: Best-of-N task pass rate
evaluation.description: The fraction of tasks solved when the system may generate N pieces of code and select the best one is used to summarize candidate stability and asymptotic task coverage.

evaluation.name: Two-task real-manipulator demonstration
evaluation.description: The system demonstrates object pushing and grasping using perception-derived object state, an AprilTag table frame, and a hardware-specific regularizer; no aggregate hardware success rate is reported.

evaluation.name: Two multi-turn steering demonstrations
evaluation.description: Four language turns shape a quadruped moonwalk and four turns sequence an apple-in-drawer behavior; the examples establish interface feasibility but not user-level reliability.

evidence.claim: The final paper appears in PMLR volume 229, pages 374-404, and reports rounded task coverage of 90% for Language to Rewards versus 50% for Code-as-Policies.
The reward is a negative weighted sum of predefined residual terms under non-negative weights and differentiable norms; LLMs modulate parameters and weights.
The translator is decomposed into a structured Motion Descriptor and a Reward Coder whose prompt contains API descriptions, an example response, and constraints.
MJPC replans actions in a receding-horizon loop; the paper uses iLQG for locomotion and Predictive Sampling for manipulation.
All experiments use GPT-4; the simulated robots are a 12-DoF quadruped and a 27-DoF manipulator comprising a 7-DoF arm and 20-DoF hand.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2 and Appendix A.3, PDF pages 5 and 14
evidence.claim: Baselines are Reward Coder without Motion Descriptor and Code-as-Policies with three hand-designed primitive skills per embodiment.

evidence.locator: Section 4.3 and Appendix A.2, PDF pages 5 and 13-14
evidence.claim: The suite has nine quadruped and eight manipulator task categories; Appendix A.2 lists instructions and expected behavior, including explicit thresholds for several manipulation tasks.

Each task-method pair uses ten generated responses and fifty MJPC evaluations per response; the full method has higher success in 11 of 17 categories, while a direct coder often omits enabling subgoals such as reaching the drawer handle.
Best-of-N pass-rate curves are used to describe task coverage and stability as more generated reward programs are available.
Two four-turn examples revise a moonwalk and sequence an apple-in-drawer task through language feedback.
The real-robot system uses F-VLM, point-cloud state estimation, an AprilTag table frame, and a hardware-specific regularizer; pushing and grasping are demonstrated.

evidence.locator: Section 5, Limitations and Future Work, PDF page 8
evidence.claim: Limitations include manually designed morphology templates, hard-to-verbalize tasks, a predefined reward vocabulary, and lack of time-varying rewards.
Full prompts expose morphology-specific templates, API signatures, phase and air-ratio bounds, code constraints, and a two-second default plan duration.

The appendix gives residual libraries and default weights; the manipulator table has an apparent XY/height label-formula mismatch and no printed orientation weight, and the real-robot residual supplies explicit thresholds.
Fifty trials are reported per generated reward; dynamic or precise tasks such as biped standing and upright banana have higher controller variance.

evidence.locator: Exact official repository commit, committed 2024-08-14 and pinned 2026-08-30
evidence.claim: The inspected official-code artifact is commit 4a3a20f9c8705e3a3ded4d218d9c129303d9682e.
The package version is 0.0.1 and its project dependencies include an unversioned OpenAI Python package.

The README pins MJPC commit c5c7ead065b7f4034ab265a13023231900dbfaa7 and states that the released robot model cannot reproduce the paper's moonwalk because the paper used unrealistically strong actuators.
The public task registry contains only Barkour and three prompt modes: thinker-coder, coder-only, and low-level.
The release selects the mutable gpt-4 model alias.

evidence.locator: prompt_thinker_coder.py lines 142-195 and process_code.py lines 29-47 at pinned commit
evidence.claim: The release performs two sequential LLM calls, extracts model-produced Python, executes it through a parameter bridge, and installs the resulting MJPC task parameters and weights.
Generated code is inserted into a Python template; emitted JSON parameters are applied only for known keys and are cast to float.
The macOS fallback explicitly warns that code is untrusted, asks for confirmation, then compiles and executes it with the local Python interpreter rather than a sandbox.
The release uses temperature 0.3 and retries outputs that still contain the CHOICE or NUM template placeholders.
